nameStory: The tooth-necked longhorn beetle gets its name from the distinctive tooth-like projections along the sides of its thorax (the middle section between head and abdomen). Like all longhorn beetles, it sports impressively long antennae that can be as long as or longer than its entire body. The 'longhorn' name comes from these antennae resembling the long horns of cattle.
description: The tooth-necked longhorn beetle is a robust, dark brown to black beetle that's part of the impressive longhorn beetle family. These substantial insects typically measure about 1-1.5 inches long, with a sturdy, somewhat flattened body. Their most striking features are their remarkably long, segmented antennae and the distinctive tooth-like spines along the edges of their thorax. Adults have a somewhat matte finish and appear quite formidable, though they're harmless to humans.

idTips.label: Thoracic teeth
idTips.description: Look for sharp, prominent tooth-like projections along the sides of the thorax (middle body section) - these feel genuinely sharp to the touch and are the beetle's signature feature

idTips.label: Long antennae
idTips.description: Antennae are thick, strongly segmented, and nearly as long as the entire body - they feel sturdy and rigid, not delicate like many other insects

idTips.label: Body color and texture
idTips.description: Dark reddish-brown to nearly black coloration with a somewhat matte, leathery-looking surface that feels smooth but not glossy

idTips.label: Size and build
idTips.description: Large and robust, about the size of your thumb, with a noticeably wide, flattened thorax that feels solid and heavy for an insect

idTips.label: Wing covers
idTips.description: Hard wing covers (elytra) with subtle lengthwise ridges you can feel with your fingertip, covering most of the abdomen

habitat: Look for tooth-necked longhorn beetles in mature deciduous and mixed forests throughout New England, particularly where oak, maple, and other hardwood trees are abundant. They're most commonly found around decaying logs, tree stumps, and areas with rotting wood, as their larvae develop inside dead and dying hardwood trees. Adults are often attracted to lights at night and may be spotted on tree trunks or flying clumsily around porch lights in wooded areas.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging from their woody nurseries in late spring, though they're not commonly seen until early summer.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when adults are most visible, often coming to lights at night and actively seeking mates. This is your best chance for spotting them.
seasonality.fall: Adult activity winds down significantly, though some individuals may still be encountered in early fall before the first hard frosts.
seasonality.winter: Adults have died off, but larvae continue developing inside dead wood, slowly growing over multiple years before emerging as adults.

funFact: The larvae of tooth-necked longhorn beetles can live inside rotting logs for up to three years, growing slowly and helping to break down dead wood into rich soil - they're like tiny, hidden lumberjacks working around the clock to recycle the forest!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with its close relative, the broad-necked root borer, but the tooth-necked species has much more prominent and sharper thoracic spines. Memory trick: 'Tooth-necked has TRUE teeth' - the spines are noticeably sharper and more tooth-like than the broader, less pronounced projections on the broad-necked species.
contextualKnowledge: Despite their fierce appearance and sharp thoracic 'teeth,' these beetles are completely harmless to humans and actually beneficial to forest ecosystems. The intimidating spines are primarily defensive, helping protect them from predators, and they cannot bite or sting people.
compareHints: The tooth-necked longhorn beetle differs from its close relative, the broad-necked root borer, primarily in the shape and prominence of the thoracic projections - tooth-necked has sharper, more pronounced 'teeth' while broad-necked has broader, less acute angles. The tooth-necked species also tends to be slightly smaller and darker overall. Both species share the impressive long antennae and robust build typical of the Prionus genus.

relatedSpecies.distinction: The closely related Tooth-necked Longhorn Beetle has distinctive tooth-like projections along the sides of its thorax, while the Broad-necked Root Borer has smooth, rounded edges on its broad thorax.
